title: Διογένης ὁδοιπορῶν
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 98 (= Perry 247). Text as printed, including Chambry's editorial punctuation (« », ⟨ ⟩ for editorial supplements). Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.t: Διογένης ὁ κύων ὁδοιπορῶν, ὡς ἐγένετο κατά τινα ποταμὸν πλημμυροῦντα, εἱστήκει πρὸς τῇ βαλβίδι ἀμηχανῶν.
sentences.tr: Diogenēs ho kyōn hodoiporōn, hōs egeneto kata tina potamon plēmmyrounta, heistēkei pros tēi balbidi amēchanōn.
sentences.l: Diogenes the Dog, travelling on foot, when he came to be at a river in flood, was standing at the brink with no way out.
sentences.i: Diogenes the Dog, on a journey, came to a river in flood and stood at the brink, at a loss.
sentences.n: ὁ κύων, 'the Dog', is Diogenes' nickname and the source of the word Cynic (κυνικός, dog-like). εἱστήκει is the pluperfect of ἵστημι with the force of an imperfect, since the perfect ἕστηκα already means 'I stand'. βαλβίς is properly the starting-line of a race-course, used here for the water's edge. ἀμηχανῶν is 'having no contrivance' — his state while he stands.

sentences.t: Εἷς δέ τις τῶν διαβιβάζειν εἰθισμένων θεασάμενος αὐτὸν διαποροῦντα, προσελθὼν καὶ ἀράμενος αὐτόν, σὺν φιλοφροσύνῃ διεπέρασεν αὐτόν.
sentences.tr: Heis de tis tōn diabibazein eithismenōn theasamenos auton diaporounta, proselthōn kai aramenos auton, syn philophrosynēi dieperasen auton.
sentences.l: And a certain one of those accustomed to carrying people across, having seen him at a loss, having come up and having lifted him, with kindliness carried him over.
sentences.i: One of the men accustomed to carrying people across saw his difficulty, came up, took him up, and ferried him over with a good grace.
sentences.n: εἰθισμένων is the perfect participle of ἐθίζω, 'those who have been made accustomed' — men who did this at a ford as a matter of course. διαποροῦντα is a supplementary participle after θεασάμενος, giving what he saw him doing. Another aorist-participle chain with the finite verb held to the end.

sentences.t: Ὁ δὲ εἱστήκει τὴν αὐτοῦ πενίαν μεμφόμενος, δι᾽ ἣν ἀμείψασθαι τὸν εὐεργέτην οὐ δύναται.
sentences.tr: Ho de heistēkei tēn autou penian memphomenos, di’ hēn ameipsasthai ton euergetēn ou dynatai.
sentences.l: And he stood blaming his own poverty, on account of which he is not able to requite his benefactor.
sentences.i: And he stood there blaming his own poverty, on account of which he could not repay his benefactor.
sentences.n: τὴν αὐτοῦ, with the article, is 'his own'. ἀμείβομαι in the middle is 'to repay, to requite'. δύναται is present where English wants a past: the narrator slips for a moment into the man's own thought.

sentences.t: Ἔτι δὲ αὐτοῦ ταῦτα διανοουμένου, ἐκεῖνος θεασάμενος ἕτερον ὁδοιπόρον διελθεῖν μὴ δυνάμενον, προσδραμὼν καὶ αὐτὸν διεπέρασε.
sentences.tr: Eti de autou tauta dianooumenou, ekeinos theasamenos heteron hodoiporon dielthein mē dynamenon, prosdramōn kai auton dieperase.
sentences.l: And while he was still turning these things over, that man, having seen another traveller unable to get across, having run up, carried him over too.
sentences.i: And while he was still turning this over, the other man saw a second traveller unable to get across, ran up, and carried him over too.
sentences.n: Genitive absolute in the present for the thought still going on. καὶ αὐτόν is 'him too', not 'himself'. μή rather than οὐ with the participle is the regular usage where the participle gives a type or a condition rather than a particular fact: anyone unable to cross.

sentences.t: Καὶ ὁ Διογένης προσελθὼν αὐτῷ εἶπεν· « Ἀλλ᾽ ἔγωγε οὐκέτι σοι χάριν ἔχω ἐπὶ τῷ γεγονότι· ὁρῶ γὰρ ὅτι οὐ κρίσει, ἀλλὰ νόσῳ αὐτὸ ποιεῖς. »
sentences.tr: Kai ho Diogenēs proselthōn autōi eipen· « All’ egōge ouketi soi charin echō epi tōi gegonoti· horō gar hoti ou krisei, alla nosōi auto poieis. »
sentences.l: And Diogenes, having come up to him, said: « Well, I at least no longer have gratitude to you for what has happened; for I see that you do it not by judgement, but by disease. »
sentences.i: And Diogenes went up to him and said: « Then I owe you no more thanks for what was done; for I see that you do it not out of judgement but out of a sickness. »
sentences.n: χάριν ἔχω with a dative is the ordinary idiom for 'I am grateful to someone'. ἔγωγε is ἐγώ intensified, 'I at any rate'. τῷ γεγονότι is a perfect participle used as a noun, 'the thing that has come about'. κρίσει and νόσῳ are datives of cause: not a considered choice but a compulsion. νόσος covers any disorder of body or mind — here the man's indiscriminate helpfulness.

sentences.t: Ὁ μῦθος δηλοῖ ὅτι ⟨οἱ⟩ μετὰ τῶν σπουδαίων καὶ τοὺς ἀνεπιτηδείους εὐεργετοῦντες οὐκ εὐεργεσίας δόξαν, ἀλογιστίας δὲ μᾶλλον ὀφλισκάνουσι.
sentences.tr: Ho mythos dēloi hoti ⟨hoi⟩ meta tōn spoudaiōn kai tous anepitēdeious euergetountes ouk euergesias doxan, alogistias de mallon ophliskanousi.
sentences.l: The fable shows that ⟨those⟩ who along with the worthy do good to the unsuitable as well incur a reputation not for beneficence, but rather for want of judgement.
sentences.i: The fable shows that those who benefit the unfit along with the deserving earn themselves a name not for generosity but for want of sense.
sentences.n: The article οἱ inside ⟨ ⟩ is Chambry's own supplement, added to turn the participle into a substantive, 'those who do good'. ὀφλισκάνω is the courtroom verb for incurring a judgement against oneself, hence 'to incur' a reputation. μετὰ τῶν σπουδαίων is the point of the moral: the fault is not the helping but the failure to distinguish.
